title: Functions and graphs you will actually use
hook: A flow meter's pressure-difference cell sends 12 mA on its 4 to 20 mA loop, exactly halfway up the signal. Why is the flow through the pipe only about 71% of full?
oneBreath: A function is a machine that turns each input into exactly one output, and its graph is every input plotted against what it gives. Five shapes, the line, square, cube, one-over and square root, sit behind laws you use at work, and some take only certain inputs or give only certain outputs. Sliding, stretching or flipping a graph changes its rule in a way you can predict, chaining two machines feeds one's output into the next, and running a machine backwards is the rearranging you already do.

ideas.title: The function machine
ideas.oneLine: A function is a rule that gives exactly one output for each input, and f(5), said "f of 5", is what comes out when 5 goes in.

ideas.title: Reading a graph as a function
ideas.oneLine: Read a function's graph by going up from an input to the curve and across to its one output, and back from an output to its inputs.

ideas.title: Five families of graphs
ideas.oneLine: Five graph shapes, the line, square, cube, one-over and square root, each have a tell-tale look, and each fits a law from your work.

ideas.title: Domain and range
ideas.oneLine: The domain is the inputs a function will take and the range is the outputs it gives, seen as its graph's spread along each axis.

ideas.title: Shifting a graph
ideas.oneLine: Adding outside the bracket, f(x) + 3, slides a graph up 3, and changing the input inside, f(x − 3), slides it 3 right.

ideas.title: Stretching and flipping
ideas.oneLine: Multiplying the output, 2f(x), stretches a graph up and down, a minus flips it over the x-axis, and multiplying the input, f(2x), squeezes it sideways.

ideas.title: One machine feeding another
ideas.oneLine: In a chain of two functions, written f(g(x)), the output of g becomes the input of f, and swapping the order usually changes the answer.

ideas.title: Undoing a machine
ideas.oneLine: An inverse function, read "f inverse", undoes a function that never gives two inputs the same output, running its steps backwards in reverse order.

calibration.q: A machine doubles whatever goes in, then adds 1. What comes out if you feed it a + 1 instead of a number?
calibration.why: The whole of a + 1 goes in, so doubling gives 2a + 2, and adding 1 gives 2a + 3. 2a + 2 doubles only the a and not the 1 that came with it, and 2a + 1 feeds in a on its own.

calibration.q: A graph shows a tank's water level against time. The line climbs, then runs flat for a while. What does the flat part tell you?
options: The tank's top is flat there
The water was running out fast
The level stayed the same for that time
calibration.why: The graph is level against time, not a picture of the tank, so a flat stretch means time passed while the level did not change. Reading it as the tank's flat top treats it as a drawing, and running out would make the line fall.
